summary: Lancaster sprawls across the western Antelope Valley floor at roughly 2,300 feet of elevation, where the Mojave Desert meets the last folds of the San Gabriel Mountains — meaning you get enormous, unobstructed skies, an average of 10.6 hours of sunshine per day, and winter nights that dip cool enough to remind you this is high desert, not the LA Basin below. That Basin matters, because Lancaster functions heavily as a bedroom community: Edwards Air Force Base and Northrop Grumman's Palmdale operations anchor the local aerospace and defense sector, but tens of thousands of commuters face a grueling drive south through the Angeles National Forest via Highway 14 to reach jobs in greater Los Angeles. At a median home price of $409,100 against a median household income of about $76,000, the price-to-income ratio sits near 5.4 — far more accessible than coastal Southern California, which is precisely why the city has grown so rapidly, though a $1,696 median rent still claims a meaningful share of that income. The city covers nearly 95 square miles at a modest density of roughly 1,850 people per square mile, which translates to wide, car-dependent arterials separating residential tracts rather than a compact walkable core, though the California Poppy Reserve sits just west of town and the spring wildflower bloom is one of the most spectacular natural displays in the state. Lancaster is, at its core, a place where Mojave space and LA-area wages meet — and the commute is the price of admission.
